questions.question: An object at rest will remain at rest unless acted upon by:
questions.explanation: This is Newton's First Law of Motion (Law of Inertia). An object at rest stays at rest unless an unbalanced (net) force acts on it. Gravity and friction are types of forces, but the fundamental principle requires an unbalanced force to change motion.
steps: Recall Newton's First Law: objects resist changes in motion
Identify that 'unbalanced force' is the general term
Eliminate specific force types (gravity, friction) as they're too narrow
Velocity is motion itself, not a cause
questions.fastStrategy: Newton's First Law always involves 'unbalanced force' or 'net force'.

questions.question: If a car travels 60 miles in 2 hours, what is its average speed?
questions.explanation: Average speed = distance ÷ time. Here: 60 miles ÷ 2 hours = 30 miles per hour.
questions.fastStrategy: Speed = distance/time. Divide total distance by total time.

questions.question: Which of Newton's laws explains why passengers lurch forward when a car suddenly stops?
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law (Inertia) states that objects in motion tend to stay in motion. When the car stops, passengers continue moving forward due to inertia until restrained by seatbelts or contact with the dashboard.
steps: Identify the phenomenon: bodies continue motion when vehicle stops
Recall that inertia is resistance to change in motion
Eliminate F=ma (that's about force and acceleration) and action-reaction
questions.fastStrategy: Inertia questions involve resistance to changes in motion—always First Law.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of force is the Newton (N). One Newton is the force required to accelerate 1 kilogram of mass at 1 meter per second squared (from F = ma).
steps: Joule = energy, Watt = power, Pascal = pressure
questions.fastStrategy: Force is measured in Newtons. Remember F = ma.

questions.question: If you push a box with 10 N of force and it accelerates at 2 m/s², what is the mass of the box?
questions.explanation: Using Newton's Second Law: F = ma. Rearranging: m = F/a. Substitute: m = 10 N / 2 m/s² = 5 kg.
steps: Rearrange to solve for mass: m = F/a
questions.fastStrategy: F = ma. To find mass, divide force by acceleration.

questions.question: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of:
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. It measures how quickly an object's velocity is changing.
steps: Recall definition: acceleration = change in velocity / time
Position change relates to velocity, not acceleration
Force and mass don't define acceleration directly
questions.fastStrategy: Acceleration = change in velocity per unit time.

questions.question: A 50 kg person experiences a gravitational force of approximately how many Newtons on Earth? (g ≈ 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Weight (force due to gravity) = mass × gravitational acceleration. W = mg = 50 kg × 10 m/s² = 500 N.
questions.fastStrategy: Weight in Newtons ≈ mass in kg × 10 (on Earth).

questions.question: Friction is a force that:
questions.explanation: Friction opposes relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It acts to resist sliding or movement, converting kinetic energy to heat.
steps: Friction slows objects, doesn't speed them up
Friction acts on both moving and stationary objects (static vs kinetic)
questions.fastStrategy: Friction always opposes motion between surfaces.

questions.question: When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with equal force. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When you push on the wall (action), the wall pushes back with equal force (reaction).
steps: Identify paired forces: you push wall, wall pushes you
Eliminate First Law (inertia) and Second Law (F=ma)
questions.fastStrategy: Equal and opposite forces = Newton's Third Law (action-reaction).

questions.question: What happens to an object's velocity if a constant net force is applied in the direction of motion?
questions.explanation: A constant net force causes constant acceleration (F = ma). Acceleration in the direction of motion increases velocity over time.
steps: Recall F = ma: force causes acceleration
Force in direction of motion → positive acceleration
questions.fastStrategy: Force in direction of motion always increases velocity.

questions.question: A lever is an example of a:
questions.explanation: A lever is one of the six classical simple machines. Simple machines multiply force or change its direction using basic mechanical principles.
steps: Recall the six simple machines: lever, pulley, wheel/axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw
Lever is on this fundamental list
Simple machines have no power source
questions.fastStrategy: Lever, pulley, inclined plane = simple machines.

questions.question: Work is defined as:
questions.explanation: Work = Force × Distance (when force and distance are in the same direction). Work is measured in Joules.
steps: Force × time is impulse, not work
questions.fastStrategy: Work = Force × Distance. Both in same direction.

questions.question: If a 20 N force moves an object 5 meters, how much work is done?
questions.explanation: Work = Force × Distance. W = 20 N × 5 m = 100 Joules.
questions.fastStrategy: Multiply force by distance to get work in Joules.

questions.question: Power is defined as:
questions.explanation: Power = Work/Time, or the rate at which work is done. It's measured in Watts (1 Watt = 1 Joule/second).
steps: Power is rate of doing work
Force × velocity also equals power (alternative formula)
Energy stored is potential/kinetic energy, not power
questions.fastStrategy: Power = Work/Time. Measured in Watts.

questions.question: An object moving at constant velocity has:
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means no change in speed or direction. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so if velocity is constant, acceleration is zero.
steps: Constant velocity = no change in velocity
If no change in velocity, then change = 0
questions.fastStrategy: Constant velocity always means zero acceleration.

questions.question: Which quantity is a vector?
questions.explanation: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity is a vector (speed with direction). Speed, mass, and energy are scalars (magnitude only).
steps: Recall: vectors have magnitude AND direction
Mass and energy have no direction
questions.fastStrategy: Velocity, force, acceleration = vectors. Speed, mass, energy = scalars.

questions.question: A pulley system is used to:

choices.B: Change the direction of force or reduce effort force

questions.explanation: Pulleys are simple machines that change the direction of applied force or provide mechanical advantage (reducing effort force needed). They don't increase work or eliminate friction.
steps: Recall purpose of simple machines: make work easier
Pulleys redirect force or multiply force
Friction exists but is minimized, not eliminated
questions.fastStrategy: Pulleys change force direction or reduce effort—don't create energy.

questions.question: If an object's speed doubles, its kinetic energy:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy = ½mv². Since velocity is squared, doubling speed (v → 2v) makes KE become ½m(2v)² = ½m(4v²) = 4 times the original KE.
steps: If v doubles: new KE = ½m(2v)²
questions.fastStrategy: KE depends on v². Double speed → 4× the energy.

questions.question: Potential energy depends on:
questions.explanation: Gravitational potential energy depends on height (position). Elastic potential energy depends on compression/stretch (configuration). Both relate to position or state, not motion.
steps: Elastic PE relates to spring compression (configuration)
Speed relates to kinetic energy, not potential
Color and temperature aren't mechanical energy factors
questions.fastStrategy: Potential energy = position (height) or configuration (springs).

questions.question: Conservation of energy states that energy:
questions.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another. Total energy in a closed system remains constant.
steps: Recall conservation principle: total energy constant
Energy transforms (PE ↔ KE) but total stays same
Energy can be transferred between objects
Energy exists in many forms (kinetic, potential, thermal, etc.)
questions.fastStrategy: Energy is conserved—never created or destroyed, only transformed.

questions.question: An inclined plane reduces the effort force needed to lift an object by:

choices.B: Increasing the distance over which force is applied
choices.C: Decreasing the mass of the object

questions.explanation: An inclined plane trades distance for force. You push over a longer distance (along the ramp) but with less force than lifting straight up. Work = Force × Distance remains constant.
steps: Recall simple machine principle: trade force for distance
Smaller force over longer distance does same work
questions.fastStrategy: Inclined plane: longer distance, less force. Work stays same.

questions.question: Momentum is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Momentum (p) = mass × velocity. It's a vector quantity measured in kg·m/s.
steps: Force × time = impulse, Force × distance = work
questions.fastStrategy: Momentum = mass × velocity. Symbol: p = mv.

questions.question: If no external forces act on a system, momentum is:
questions.explanation: The Law of Conservation of Momentum states that in a closed system with no external forces, total momentum remains constant. Momentum can be transferred between objects but the total doesn't change.
steps: No external force → total momentum constant
Momentum can redistribute but total conserved
This applies to collisions and explosions
questions.fastStrategy: No external forces → momentum is conserved (constant total).

questions.question: Centripetal force:

choices.A: Pushes objects outward in circular motion
choices.B: Pulls objects toward the center of circular motion

questions.explanation: Centripetal force is the inward force that keeps an object moving in a circular path. It always points toward the center of the circle (like tension in a string or friction on a road).
steps: Force must point inward to maintain circular path
Outward feeling is centrifugal (apparent force, not real)
Circular motion requires continuous inward force
questions.fastStrategy: Centripetal force always points toward center of circular motion.

questions.question: The mechanical advantage of a machine is the ratio of:
questions.explanation: Mechanical Advantage (MA) = Output Force / Input Force. It tells you how much a machine multiplies the applied force. MA > 1 means force is multiplied.
steps: Work ratio is efficiency, not MA
questions.fastStrategy: MA = Output force ÷ Input force. Measures force multiplication.
